name: Body fat calipers

lead: Skinfold calipers let you track body fat at home so you can see whether a cut or bulk is actually changing your physique. They are cheap and need no appointment.

The caliper applies standard pressure to a pinched fold of skin and fat at set body sites. The readings go into a formula such as Durnin-Womersley or Jackson-Pollock to estimate body density, and a second equation such as Siri or Brozek turns density into a body fat percentage. The method is long established in sports science, and sources describe it as best for following change over time in one person rather than giving a true absolute figure.

paras: Lifters measure the same sites, often a handful on the torso and thigh, at the same time of day with the same technique, then log the sum or the estimated percentage every week or two. Many compare the trend with the mirror, photos and the scale.

No physical risk. Accuracy depends on site placement, pressure, caliper type and the formula used. It captures only fat under the skin, not visceral fat, and two people with similar readings can differ in total body fat.

angle.text: Lifters pinch set sites with calipers to estimate body fat and track whether a cut or bulk is changing their physique. The method is long established in sports science, and users mostly value it for tracking changes rather than absolute numbers.

lead: Body fat calipers, also called skinfold calipers or plicometers, are hand-held instruments that measure the thickness of a pinched fold of skin and the fat beneath it at standardized body sites. The readings are used in equations that estimate whole-body fat percentage. The method is also known as the pinch test.[1]

Reference methods such as the Durnin-Womersley and Jackson-Pollock formulas estimate body density from skinfold sums, and a second formula such as Siri or Brozek converts density to body fat percentage, which compounds the statistical error.[1] Accuracy depends on precise site placement and consistent pressure, and sources describe the method as better for tracking change within one person than for giving a true absolute figure.[1]

Validation studies have compared skinfold calipers with ultrasound and computed tomography for subcutaneous fat measurement, and a 1979 study examined how compressible skinfolds are, one reason caliper readings vary.[2][3]
infobox: Three to seven, depending on formula
Non-medical measuring tool; no clearance needed for typical consumer use

paras: The examiner pinches a fold of skin and underlying fat at a defined site, applies the caliper jaws, and reads the thickness. Formulas use between three and seven sites. The number of sites is reported to matter less than an individual's own fat distribution.[1]

Because the sum of skinfolds predicts body density rather than fat directly, a conversion equation is applied, and population-specific equations may be less accurate for people outside the group on which they were developed, such as highly athletic older people.[1]

A comparison of skinfold calipers, ultrasound and computed tomography for subcutaneous fat measurement examined how well the methods agree.[3] An earlier study examined how compressible skinfolds are, which affects the reading depending on tissue and pressure.[2] Research that used skinfolds, ultrasound and body mass index to characterize the subcutaneous fat layer has been used in electromyography studies as a correction factor.[4]

Wikipedia notes the technique measures only subcutaneous fat, not visceral fat, so similar readings can correspond to different total body fat, and that results vary with caliper type and examiner technique.[1] It also states that the method may not give a true body fat reading but reliably tracks change when the same person uses the same technique.[1]

Calipers are discussed in bodybuilding and physique communities as a low-cost way to follow fat loss during a cut and to compare against scale weight. Users often prefer them to bioimpedance scales, citing consumer pricing and portability. Caliper types range from inexpensive plastic pinch devices to spring-loaded metal models, and the reliability of the reading depends on a consistent operator.

No clinical trials of calipers as an intervention were found. Methodological studies have compared skinfold calipers with ultrasound and computed tomography for measuring subcutaneous fat, and have examined how skinfold compressibility affects readings.[2][3] A 1962 paper described the measurement of total body fat with skinfold calipers.[5]

lore.intro: Calipers are a recurring tool in fitness communities for tracking body fat during cutting phases.
